Here at Boss Design Center, we are as committed to getting your kitchen remodel, basement finishing, bathroom remodel, and room addition started and finished as you are, so call our expert team of remodelers who are standing by to deliver quality results from Northern Virginia to the District of Columbia to Maryland. More than just a business in these areas, we consider ourselves neighbors and community members.

Fully licensed, bonded, and insured, you can rely on our professionalism to deliver the results that you were looking for when you first began looking for contractors to help realize your remodeling ambitions.

While we are more than happy to replace those aging kitchen cabinets, the scope of our vision exceeds those small ambitions, and as our name implies at Boss Design Center, we take a keen interest in the entire design process from drawing board to completion. We have great ideas to help you realize your remodeling dreams from that room addition to the ultimate kitchen remodeling; we bring ten years of experience to the design table and construction site.

Contact us today and let’s start planning that dream home remodeling project.

KITCHEN REMODELING

The kitchen is at the heart of the home, and making sure that that heart is beating as strongly as you want it to beat means stepping back and looking at ways it might benefit from a remodel.

BATHROOM REMODELING

If you talk to a real estate agent, they will tell you that bathroom remodeling is the best bang for your buck. One of the things about a bathroom remodeling effort is that it is better to do it sooner rather than latter, so you can maximize the amount of enjoyment you get from the experience.

HOME ADDITION

If you have bigger dreams for your home, it may be time to consider adding square footage to your floor plan. At Boss Design Center, it’s our mission to make luxury affordable for home additions in Virginia, Maryland, and Washington D.C., with the highest standard of craftsmanship at every stage.

BASEMENT REMODELING

If you’re living in Northern Virginia, DC, or Maryland, and have come to the conclusion that the space beneath your home would be more charitably called a “root cellar” than a basement and you are looking for a little less root and a lot more cellar, call us here at Boss Design Center to let us help your basement finishing efforts become a reality.

CONDO REMODELING

A condo renovation often is subject to more stringent requirements. Our experienced team can educate you on what to expect during a condo remodel and how to best plan for your project.

DO YOU NEED A PERMIT TO REMODEL YOUR HOME IN VIRGINIA? 2026 GUIDE
DO YOU NEED A PERMIT TO REMODEL YOUR HOME IN VIRGINIA? 2026 GUIDE
by Talha Gursoy Boss Design Update October 19, 2026

Do you need a permit to remodel your home in Virginia? If the work moves a wall, changes plumbing or electrical, finishes a basement, or adds square footage, yes. If the work is cosmetic, you usually don’t. Replacing cabinets, countertops, flooring, paint, and fixtures in the spots they already occupy is exempt across the state. Permits follow the work, not the label. Moving a sink three feet counts. Repainting the same kitchen doesn’t.

Virginia runs one building code statewide, the Virginia Uniform Statewide Building Code, written by the Virginia Department of Housing and Community Development. Your county or city building department is the office that reviews the plans, issues the permit, and inspects the work. That’s why a neighbor’s experience in Arlington tells you almost nothing about how your project will go in Loudoun.

At Boss Design Center, permitting is step seven of our ten step process, and we budget four to six weeks between the signed construction contract and the first day of demolition. We pull the permits, price the fees into your contract, schedule the inspections, and deal with the building department. We’ve been remodeling in the D.C. metro area for over a decade, and the permit itself rarely slows a project down. Not planning for it does.

WHICH BUILDING CODE APPLIES TO REMODELING IN VIRGINIA IN 2026?

The 2021 edition of the Virginia Uniform Statewide Building Code took effect on January 18, 2024. It adopts the 2021 International Codes and the 2020 National Electrical Code, and every permit pulled today is reviewed against it.

The code applies everywhere in Virginia. The jurisdictions used as examples below are Northern Virginia, because that’s where we work, but the same questions apply to any local building department.

The edition matters when you research your project online. Plenty of pages still describe the 2011 or 2018 editions and still rank well. Check the date on anything you read, including this one.

The code splits into three parts: new construction, alterations to existing buildings, and ongoing maintenance. A remodel falls almost entirely under the second, the Virginia Existing Building Code.

WHAT REMODELING WORK REQUIRES A PERMIT IN VIRGINIA?

The state code lists the work you can’t start without a permit in hand. For a residential remodel, these are the triggers:

Removing a wall or any part of one, or adding a new one
Any structural change, including a new beam, a new header, or a wider opening
Changing the water supply, drain, or vent lines
Any new or relocated electrical wiring
Fire protection systems, mechanical systems, and anything fueled by gas or oil
Reworking how people get out of the house in an emergency, such as a stairway or an exit path
Repairing or replacing an assembly rated to slow fire or smoke, which in a house usually means the separation between an attached garage and the rooms beside it

Changing how the building is used, certain lot line adjustments, and disturbing asbestos during construction or demolition also require permits. The full list sits in Virginia’s permit requirements.

Note the first item. Wall removal counts whether the wall carries load or not. Fairfax County spells that out on its own permit requirements page, which expressly covers non load bearing and non structural walls. Adding a circuit for a new induction range is on the list too.

WHAT REMODELING WORK IS EXEMPT FROM A PERMIT?

The same section of the state code exempts a specific list of ordinary repairs. The ones that come up in remodeling are:

Floor finishes
Cabinetry and trim
Paint and wallpaper
Plumbing fixtures, as long as the supply, drain, and vent lines stay where they are
Snap switches, dimmers, standard 15 and 20 amp receptacles, light fixtures, and ceiling fans
Mechanical appliances, but only where the equipment isn’t fueled by gas or oil
Windows and doors that match the existing ones in operation and opening size and don’t require changes to the framed opening
Roof covering and siding replacement on most homes, where design wind speed is not greater than 100 mph

Outside the house, sheds up to 256 square feet, most fences, masonry walls up to six feet, and retaining walls holding back less than three feet of fill are also exempt.

Two qualifiers apply to that exempt list. Exempt work still has to meet the rest of the code, so no permit doesn’t mean no rules. And the building official can require a permit for anything they don’t consider minor and ordinary, or waive one that’s genuinely trivial. Borderline calls belong to that official, not to your contractor and not to a blog.

WHICH COMMON REMODELING PROJECTS NEED A PERMIT?

The table below sorts the work we see most often on kitchen, bathroom, basement, and whole house projects in Northern Virginia. It follows the state code, with Fairfax County’s published list as the local example.

PROJECT	PERMIT NEEDED?	WHY
Cabinet and countertop replacement	No	Exempt as cabinetry and trim
Flooring or tile replacement	No	Exempt as floor finishes
Paint and wallpaper	No	Exempt
Like for like fixture swap in the same spot	Usually no	Exempt if supply, drain, and vent lines are untouched
Window or door swap in the same opening	Usually no	Only if operation and opening size match and the framed opening is unchanged
Re-siding or roof shingle replacement	Usually no	Exempt on most homes, with a historic district exception
Shed 256 square feet or less	No	Exempt statewide
Removing or adding a wall	Yes	Covered by the code whether it’s load bearing or not
Structural change, new beam or opening	Yes	Structural component
New, relocated, or repaired electrical	Yes	Electric wiring
Relocated plumbing	Yes	Alters supply, drain, or vent lines
HVAC, ductwork, gas appliances, range hoods	Yes	Mechanical and fuel supply systems
Water heater or appliance replacement in place	Depends	State exempts appliances not fueled by gas or oil; Fairfax lists appliance replacement as permit required
New or enlarged window or door opening	Yes	Changes the framed opening
Finishing a basement	Yes	Interior alteration, usually with trade permits
Creating a bedroom	Yes	Egress, light, and ventilation requirements apply
Deck or addition	Yes	Building permit, plus zoning review

The water heater row is where jurisdictions split. Fairfax County lists direct replacement of household appliances, including stoves, ovens, water heaters, and HVAC, as permit required. The state code exempts mechanical appliance replacement where the equipment isn’t gas or oil fueled, and Fairfax’s own exempt list includes like for like mechanical replacement with no change of location. The county page reads both ways depending on which line you land on. The building official settles it, which is a good argument for asking rather than assuming.

DOES A KITCHEN OR BATHROOM REMODEL NEED A PERMIT IN VIRGINIA?

Almost always, yes. A kitchen remodel that keeps every cabinet, appliance, and fixture in its original location is exempt, and that project is rare. Most kitchens we design move the sink, relocate the range, add circuits for new appliances, vent a hood to the exterior, or take out the wall between the kitchen and the dining room. Any one of those pulls the project into permit territory.

The same goes for a bathroom remodel. Swapping a vanity for one that lines up with the existing drain is exempt. Converting a tub to a curbless shower, moving the toilet, or adding a heated floor is not.

Fairfax County is explicit about the big ones, listing kitchen renovations, bathroom remodels, finished basements, and new bedrooms as permit required interior alterations. When a homeowner tells us their kitchen project is just cosmetic, it usually isn’t, once we walk the space and see where the plumbing and the panel actually are.

DO ELECTRICAL, PLUMBING, AND HVAC NEED SEPARATE PERMITS?

Usually yes, and this is the part that surprises people. State code allows building, plumbing, electrical, mechanical, and special construction permits to be issued separately or combined. In Northern Virginia they’re generally separate records, each with its own rough-in and final inspection.

In Fairfax, the electrical, plumbing, and mechanical permits are pulled after the building permit is issued and reference it as the parent permit. HVAC work may also call for a residential HVAC certification.
In Arlington, mechanical, plumbing, and electrical applications are submitted separately and issued based on the work shown on the approved building permit drawings. Fire protection work needs its own permit and plans.
In Loudoun, residential trade permits are separate, and since October 1, 2025, some residential fuel gas permits require a plan review.

So a kitchen isn’t one permit. It’s a building permit plus a trade permit for each system you touch, each with inspections that have to happen in sequence. That sequence, more than the plan review, is what drives the construction calendar.

DOES A REMODEL NEED ARCHITECT STAMPED DRAWINGS IN VIRGINIA?

Most single family remodels don’t. Under Virginia’s professional seal requirements, plans for single family and two family homes, townhouses, and multifamily buildings up to three stories don’t need an architect or engineer seal. Electrical and mechanical systems are the exception, and the drawings still have to carry the author’s name, address, and occupation.

A seal is required when the work changes the occupancy or occupant load, modifies the structural system, changes access or egress, increases the fire hazard, or involves a unique structural design affecting floors, roofs, walls, or foundations.

In practice, a straightforward kitchen or bathroom needs no stamp. Pulling out a bearing wall or building an addition typically does, because the structural system is being modified. We bring structural engineering in during design so the stamped drawings are ready when the application goes in.

CAN A HOMEOWNER PULL THEIR OWN PERMIT IN VIRGINIA?

Yes, for their own primary residence, within limits. A lot of contractor websites say otherwise, and they’re wrong.

Code of Virginia 54.1-1111 requires a permit applicant to provide either proof of a valid contractor license or a written statement that they aren’t subject to licensing. It doesn’t bar homeowners. The licensing exemption itself sits in 54.1-1101, which covers a person performing or supervising work on no more than one primary residence they own and use, in any 24 month period. Localities handle it through a notarized owner exemption affidavit.

Two real limits apply. The exemption covers general contractor licensing only, so electrical, plumbing, HVAC, and gas work still has to be performed by a state licensed tradesman. And the permit holder is the party the building official holds responsible for the work, the inspections, and any notice of violation.

That second point is what matters on a project of any size. Fairfax allows property owners to obtain permits in their own names while strongly recommending that a licensed contractor pull the permit as the responsible party. If a contractor asks you to pull the permit on a six figure remodel, that tells you something about their licensing, or about who they expect to answer for the work. It’s one of the practical differences between a design-build firm and a crew assembled job by job.

CHECK THAT THE LICENSE CLASS COVERS YOUR PROJECT

Virginia contractor licenses come in three classes, and the class is tied to project value. The current thresholds are:

CLASS	PROJECT LIMIT	ANNUAL LIMIT
Class C	Less than $30,000 per project	Less than $250,000 in 12 months
Class B	Less than $150,000 per project	Less than $1 million in 12 months
Class A	No monetary limit	No monetary limit

A license is required for any work valued over $1,000. Our own kitchen projects run $80,000 to $250,000, a range that sits right on top of the Class B ceiling. Verify the class, not just that a license exists, through the DPOR license lookup. Many third party sites still publish outdated thresholds of $120,000 and $10,000. Our guide to choosing a remodeling firm covers the rest of what to check before you sign anything.

HOW LONG DOES PERMIT REVIEW TAKE IN NORTHERN VIRGINIA?

Published review times are shorter than most homeowners expect, and vary by jurisdiction and by whether your project qualifies for an expedited track.

JURISDICTION	PUBLISHED REVIEW APPROACH
Fairfax County	Fast Track residential plan review dropped from 5 business days to 1 business day in April 2026, for eligible projects
Arlington County	5 business days for a residential alteration, 10 for an addition, 2 business days for projects meeting express criteria
Loudoun County	Intake completeness check in 2 to 5 business days for County Typical decks, basements, and trades, up to 10 business days for other residential permits
City of Alexandria	Standard residential plan review, with walk-through service for qualifying projects

Read those published times as approximate and eligibility dependent. Fairfax Fast Track covers finished basements, decks, minor interior alterations, one story additions of 500 square feet or less, garages, and sheds, and the county asks applicants to confirm eligibility with staff before submitting. Arlington’s express criteria are specific: under 750 square feet of work, one story, no removal of load bearing walls on a nonconforming building, no more than three toilets, and several more. Miss one and you’re on the standard track.

Review time also isn’t door to door time. Arlington notes roughly two business days at intake for a completeness check, two for final processing and fee calculation, and two for release of the approved plan set. A five day review is realistically closer to two calendar weeks from submission to a permit in hand. Trade permits and any zoning, floodplain, or Resource Protection Area review stack on top of that.

Fees are calculated on construction value and differ by jurisdiction. Loudoun’s published fee schedule is the clearest example. A residential alteration runs 1 percent of construction cost plus a $130 plan review fee. An addition of 1,000 square feet or less is a flat $395. Treat figures for other jurisdictions as a starting point and confirm the current schedule with the building department. Under a fixed-rate contract, those fees are priced in before construction starts.

Permits also expire. The same code section that allows separate trade permits lets the building official revoke one if work doesn’t start within six months of issuance or stalls for six months, though trade permits hold as long as the building permit does.

WHEN DOES PERMITTING HAPPEN IN A REMODEL?

Permitting sits between design and demolition.

A Boss Design Center project runs in this order. Design and renderings take one to two months. Material selections happen in the showroom. The fixed-rate construction contract is signed. Permitting and scheduling follow, and that phase runs four to six weeks. Construction on a kitchen then takes three to four months, which we break down in our guide to kitchen remodel timelines. A whole house project with structural work or an addition carries a longer permitting window, because more reviews apply.

Those four to six weeks aren’t all plan review. Drawings get finalized, trade subcontractors get lined up so their permits can follow the building permit, and HOA or architectural review runs on its own calendar. Firms that treat permitting as an afterthought find this out the week they wanted to start demolition.

WHAT INSPECTIONS DOES A REMODEL REQUIRE?

Inspections happen where work is about to be covered up. An inspector can’t verify framing, wiring, or plumbing behind finished drywall.

Loudoun’s published requirements are typical. An alteration gets a framing inspection and a final. Additions add footing, foundation, insulation, and final building inspections. Each trade permit carries its own rough-in and final. Approved plans have to be on site, and inspections are scheduled at least one working day ahead.

Fairfax runs combination inspections, which means all related inspections on a project, concealment and final among them, have to be scheduled on the same day. Bundle them wrong and you get a failed inspection and a reinspection fee. Fairfax closes a residential project out with a Residential Use Permit, the county’s term for a certificate of occupancy. Arlington requires a certificate of occupancy for certain projects, such as a new house or an accessory dwelling unit, with its own application and fees.

A like for like interior alteration with no change of occupancy doesn’t produce a new certificate of occupancy. It closes out at final inspection. If you see a blanket claim that every remodel generates a new CO, that’s not how it works.

WHAT HAPPENS IF YOU REMODEL WITHOUT A PERMIT IN VIRGINIA?

The consequences rarely show up during construction. They show up later.

Penalties. Violating the building code is a misdemeanor, with a fine of up to $2,500 under Code of Virginia 36-106. Localities may also adopt a civil penalty schedule of up to $100 for the first summons and up to $350 for each additional one. Each day a violation continues counts as a separate offense, with a $4,000 cap on a series arising from the same facts.

Enforcement. A county investigator who finds unpermitted or uninspected work issues a notice of violation with a period to correct it. Correcting it usually means applying for the permit after the fact and opening up finished work so it can be inspected. Fairfax’s guidance notes that failure to comply can lead to legal action.

Insurance. Fairfax County warns that an insurance company may not cover damage or loss to a structure built without proper permits, and advises owners to check with their insurer or attorney. That’s the county’s warning rather than a universal rule, but worth taking seriously.

Resale and refinance. Virginia is a buyer beware disclosure state, and the standard residential property disclosure doesn’t ask a seller to itemize unpermitted work. That doesn’t make it invisible. It surfaces at the buyer’s inspection, the appraisal, or a refinance, usually when you have the least leverage to fix it. A basement bedroom that can’t count as living space because it was never permitted is the common version.

DOES YOUR HOA HAVE TO APPROVE THE PROJECT TOO?

HOA and architectural review approval is a separate track from the county permit, and neither one substitutes for the other. Loudoun County tells applicants directly that obtaining HOA or POA approval is their own responsibility.

In Northern Virginia this is where exterior projects lose time. Additions, decks, window changes, and siding often need architectural review committee approval, and many committees meet monthly. If yours meets in three weeks, that’s your timeline regardless of how fast the county moves. We prepare the documentation your association asks for, though most require the homeowner to submit it.

Zoning is its own check. Setbacks, lot coverage, land disturbance approval before you dig, and VDOT permits for work in the state right of way all apply independently of the building permit. Fairfax tells residential applicants that projects in the towns of Vienna or Clifton need separate approvals from those towns on top of the county’s.

DO HISTORIC DISTRICTS AND FLOOD ZONES CHANGE THE ANSWER?

Yes, in two situations, both of which can pull otherwise exempt work back into permit territory.

In a locally designated historic district, the building official may require a permit for replacement siding, roofing, and windows even though the state exempts them. In Alexandria, the Board of Architectural Review has to issue a Certificate of Appropriateness for exterior alterations visible from a public right of way, plus a permit to demolish for removal or encapsulation of more than 25 square feet of material, regardless of visibility. Check the board’s published meeting calendar early, because the hearing date sets your schedule. Interior work generally falls outside the board’s review.

In a special flood hazard area, the building official may also require permits for otherwise exempt work. Fairfax requires separate approval for improvements in a floodplain or Chesapeake Bay Resource Protection Area, and those reviews run alongside the building permit.

THE SHORT VERSION
Cosmetic work in existing locations is exempt. Structural, electrical, plumbing, mechanical, and gas work is not.
One state code, but your county or city administers it, and the building official has discretion on borderline work.
Kitchens, bathrooms, basements, and additions almost always need a building permit plus trade permits.
You can legally pull your own permit for your own primary residence, but the permit holder is the responsible party.
Published review times run from one business day to roughly two weeks door to door, and HOA, historic, and floodplain reviews run on separate clocks.
The cost of skipping a permit usually lands at resale, refinance, or an insurance claim, not during construction.

Confirm your specific scope with your local building department. The building official has the final say on what your address requires.

PLANNING A REMODEL IN VIRGINIA?

We handle permitting as part of the job at Boss Design Center, from application through final inspection. We’re licensed in Virginia, Maryland, and Washington, D.C., and we work throughout Northern Virginia from our McLean showroom at 1389 Chain Bridge Road, serving Fairfax, Arlington, Loudoun, Alexandria, Falls Church, Vienna, Great Falls, and Reston.

If you’re planning a kitchen, bathroom, basement, addition, or whole house project, schedule a consultation. We’ll walk your space, tell you what the permit picture looks like, and give you a realistic timeline before you commit to anything.

WHAT IS THE MOST EXPENSIVE PART OF A BATHROOM REMODEL IN VIRGINIA?
by Talha Gursoy Bathroom September 14, 2026

Labor is the largest cost category in a bathroom remodel, commonly running 40% to 65% of the total. The most expensive single assembly in the room is the shower, which This Old House puts at just over $8,000 on average nationally, ahead of plumbing, cabinetry and tile. In the Washington market a standardized midrange bathroom runs $25,936 and an upscale one $80,994, both marginally below the national figures. Either way you answer the question, your money goes to skilled work more than to the products you pick out.

At Boss Design Center we’ve been designing and building bathrooms across Northern Virginia since 2014, and the expensive parts of the job are almost always the parts nobody sees once it’s finished. Drain and vent lines, supply lines, the waterproofing behind the tile, the exhaust fan, and the subfloor underneath all sit behind finished surfaces. They’re also the items a bid can leave open as an allowance instead of a selected, quoted number, which is why two estimates for what looks like the same bathroom remodel in Virginia can be tens of thousands of dollars apart.

WHERE THE MONEY GOES IN A BATHROOM REMODEL

This Old House published per-component national averages for a full bathroom remodel in July 2026. These are broad national averages rather than Northern Virginia quotes, and the categories overlap, so they don’t add up to a project total. What they show clearly is the order of magnitude between components.

COMPONENT	NATIONAL AVERAGE
Complete shower installation	$8,044
Plumbing	$5,545
Cabinetry	$2,929
Insulation and drywall	$2,338
Tiling	$1,326
Bathtub	$1,123
Flooring	$1,114
Toilet	$467
Electrical	$456
Tub faucets	$423

Look at the gap between the top two lines and the bottom four. The shower and the plumbing together account for more than the toilet, the tub, the tub faucets, the flooring and the electrical combined. Homeowners tend to budget in the opposite direction, because fixtures are the part of the project you can shop for and hold in your hand. A more expensive faucet costs more than a plainer one, and that’s the end of it. A relocated drain changes demolition, framing, waterproofing, tile and inspections all at once.

How much of your total goes to labor depends on how much of that hidden work your project requires. Angi puts labor at roughly 40% to 65% of a full bathroom remodel, and This Old House’s shower analysis lands in a similar band at 40% to 60% for shower work specifically. A bathroom that keeps every fixture where it is will sit at the low end. A bathroom that moves the toilet and turns a tub alcove into a curbless shower will sit at the high end.

WHY MOVING PLUMBING FIXTURES RAISES THE COST SO MUCH

Relocating a fixture is the single decision most likely to change your budget, and it’s usually made during design, when it feels like a drawing choice rather than a cost. The published benchmarks give you a sense of the scale.

CHANGE	REPORTED COST
Floor plan change requiring plumbing and electrical rework	About $5,000
Moving a fixture three feet or more	$500 to $1,000

Those figures come from NerdWallet and Angi. They’re national planning benchmarks rather than Northern Virginia trade pricing, so use them to understand the size of the decision. They aren’t a quote for your bathroom.

The cost climbs because moving a fixture means opening the floor to reach the drain. If your bathroom sits over a crawlspace or an unfinished basement, a plumber can work from below. If it sits on a concrete slab, the slab has to be cut and repoured, and nobody publishes a credible figure for what that adds, so a contractor quoting that difference without having seen your floor is guessing at it. Once the drain moves, the vent line that serves it has to follow, the supply lines get rerun, the framing gets patched, the subfloor gets rebuilt, and the waterproofing and tile go back over all of it.

WHAT VIRGINIA’S PLUMBING CODE REQUIRES

Virginia adopted the 2021 International Plumbing Code as part of its current building code, effective January 18, 2024. Section 704.1 sets the minimum slope a horizontal drain line has to maintain.

HORIZONTAL DRAIN SIZE	VIRGINIA MINIMUM SLOPE
2.5 inches or less	1/4 inch per foot
3 to 6 inches	1/8 inch per foot
8 inches or larger	1/16 inch per foot

That requirement matters more than it sounds like it should. A drain line has to fall continuously toward the main stack, so every additional foot of horizontal run uses up vertical space inside your floor. Move a toilet far enough from the stack and there may not be enough depth left between the joists to keep the required fall. The fix at that point is a different route, a dropped ceiling in the room below, or a raised floor above, and the relocation stops being a plumbing cost and becomes a structural one. That’s the kind of problem worth solving on paper during design, where the answer is a drawing revision, instead of on site, where it’s a change order.

WHY THE SHOWER COSTS MORE THAN ANYTHING ELSE IN THE ROOM

A custom shower is a stack of separate systems, each one built correctly and in the right order, and each one carrying its own cost. The tile goes on last, and it isn’t where most of the money goes.

CUSTOM SHOWER ELEMENT	NATIONAL INSTALLED BENCHMARK
Custom shower pan	$1,500 to $3,000
Waterproofing system	$1,500 to $2,000
Tile floor installation	$2,000 to $2,500
Shower door	$600 to $900
Drain	$400 to $500
Shower head	$200 to $500
Entire custom shower remodel	$8,500 to $10,000

These come from This Old House’s 2026 shower cost analysis. The scopes overlap in places, so the individual lines won’t sum neatly to the total, and a frameless glass enclosure or a stone slab surround sits well above the door and tile figures shown here. For a closer look at what happens to these numbers at the top of the market, we cover high-end bathroom remodel costs separately.

WHAT A WATERPROOFED SHOWER ACTUALLY INCLUDES

Waterproofing is the line homeowners recognize least and the one that matters most, because it’s the only part of the assembly whose failure destroys everything built on top of it. A modern shower uses a bonded sheet or board membrane over backer board, with every seam and inside corner banded, and a sealed connection where the membrane meets the drain. The performance standard those membranes have to meet is ANSI A118.10, published by the Tile Council of North America, whose installation handbook is the reference a qualified tile setter works from.

Design choices change what that assembly costs. A curbless shower, meaning one with no step to walk over, requires recessing or sloping the subfloor toward a linear drain. That means more framing and more labor before a single tile gets set. More of our clients ask for curbless showers every year, and most of them expect it to cost less because the finished room looks simpler. It usually costs more.

WHY A SMALL BATHROOM DOES NOT COST PROPORTIONALLY LESS

A bathroom half the size of another bathroom doesn’t cost half as much, and that catches most homeowners off guard. The work doesn’t scale with the floor area.

The clearest evidence is the benchmark scope in the 2025 Cost vs. Value report from JLC and Zonda. Their midrange bathroom project is defined as an existing 5-by-7-foot bathroom, which is 35 square feet, and it includes a tub and surround, a pressure-balanced shower control, a toilet, a vanity with counter and sink, a medicine cabinet and a ceramic tile floor. In the Washington market that scope came in at $25,936. Divide it out and you get roughly $741 per square foot, which is our own calculation from their published figures rather than a number JLC reports. Per-foot rates fall as rooms get larger, which is why broader regional averages land well below this.

That per-foot figure looks absurd until you count the trades. A 35 square foot room still needs a plumber, a tile setter, an electrician, a carpenter, a drywall crew and a painter. Each one has to show up, set up, work in sequence, and come back at the end for touch-ups. The room still needs one toilet, one shower valve, one exhaust fan and one waterproofed wet area. Making the room smaller saves you some tile and some flooring. It doesn’t reduce the number of trades you’re paying to show up, and it doesn’t remove a single inspection.

WHAT TILE, VANITIES, AND FIXTURES ADD

Tile is the cost homeowners underestimate most often, because they price the tile and forget the setting. This Old House puts professional tile installation labor broadly at $3 to $15 per square foot, and the spread within that range is entirely about difficulty. Large-format porcelain needs a flatter substrate and more preparation. Mosaic needs more cuts and more grout lines per square foot. A herringbone or stacked pattern adds layout time and waste. The material invoice and the labor invoice move together, which is why a tile upgrade rarely costs only what the tile costs.

Vanities behave the same way. This Old House assigns cabinetry an average of $2,929 in its whole-bath model and puts professional vanity replacement labor at $665 to $3,300, with custom cabinet work adding roughly $500 to $2,800 in labor over a straightforward install. In a high-end Northern Virginia primary bath, none of those averages describe the actual scope. Custom widths, furniture-style construction, integrated lighting or outlets, a stone top and two sinks are a different piece of work than swapping a stock vanity.

Visible fixtures are the exception to all of this. In the same national model, the average bathtub is $1,123, tub faucets are $423 and the toilet is $467. You can spend many times those figures on a freestanding tub or a designer fitting, and plenty of our clients do. A more expensive faucet only changes one line on your estimate. Moving a drain, rebuilding a waterproofed envelope, or finding a rotted subfloor changes several lines at once, and that’s what decides whether a project lands on budget. Kitchens run on a different hierarchy, where cabinetry leads the budget rather than hidden labor.

DOES A BATHROOM REMODEL COST MORE IN NORTHERN VIRGINIA?

Less than most people assume, once you hold the scope constant. This is worth being straight about, because the local cost guides you’ve probably already read tend to assert a large regional premium without showing the data.

For a standardized scope, the Washington market runs slightly below the national figure. In the 2025 Cost vs. Value data for Washington, the midrange bathroom remodel is $25,936 against a national figure of $26,138, and the upscale bathroom remodel is $80,994 against $81,612 nationally. Both are about 0.8% below national. The same dataset tracks what comes back at resale, and recoupment falls as scope rises: 68.0% on the midrange project, 62.1% on a universal-design bath, and 40.1% on the upscale one.

The wage data points the same direction. Bureau of Labor Statistics figures for the Washington-Arlington-Alexandria area, released in July 2026, show a mean hourly wage across all occupations of $44.20 here against $33.54 nationally, a gap of about 32%. For construction and extraction occupations specifically, the gap is $32.76 against $31.42, or about 4.3%. Those are employee wages rather than what a firm charges a client, so you can’t turn them into a labor rate for your project. What they do tell you is that the trade-wage premium in this market is small.

What makes a Northern Virginia bathroom expensive is scope and service level. Cost vs. Value prices a standardized national specification, and that specification isn’t what most homeowners here are actually buying. A McLean or Great Falls primary suite with a curbless shower, a stone slab surround, custom cabinetry, heated floors and a relocated layout is a different project, and it costs what that project costs anywhere. If you want the local numbers side by side, we break down bathroom remodeling cost across the D.C. metro area in detail.

One thing that has moved recently is materials. NAHB’s second-quarter 2026 remodeling survey found that 74% of remodelers reported suppliers raising prices since March, with the average reported increase at 6.7%. That’s a national figure across all remodeling rather than a bathroom index, but it’s a good reason to be skeptical of any cost article written before this year.

PERMITS FOR A BATHROOM REMODEL IN VIRGINIA

Virginia requires a permit before you alter the water supply or distribution system, the sanitary drainage or vent system, electrical wiring, or regulated mechanical systems. Section 13VAC5-63-80 of the Virginia Administrative Code also exempts ordinary repairs, including the direct replacement of certain plumbing fixtures where the water distribution system isn’t altered.

The line between a repair and an alteration is the same line that separates an inexpensive bathroom from an expensive one. Swapping a vanity faucet in place is a repair. Moving the vanity to another wall, rerouting its drain and vent, and adding a circuit is an alteration, and it brings a permit application, an inspection schedule and coordination with the county along with the labor.

WHAT A BATHROOM PERMIT COSTS IN FAIRFAX AND LOUDOUN

Fairfax County’s 2026 fee schedule, adopted in May 2026, sets the residential plumbing permit base fee at $141.75 for one to seven fixtures, with a 2% Code Academy levy applied on top. Other jurisdictions structure it differently. Loudoun County notes that a residential project can involve a parent building permit plus separate electrical, mechanical, gas and plumbing trade permits.

HOW LONG A BATHROOM REMODEL TAKES

Nearly two-thirds of bathroom remodels run one to four weeks, with about one in five going past a month, according to This Old House’s 2026 survey of 1,000 homeowners who had remodeled. Permitting is what pushes a project toward the long end. Permits and inspections sit on the critical path, so a project that stops to wait for an approval nobody planned for is a project that runs long, and a longer project costs more.

We obtain and manage every permit for our projects, including the applications, the fees and the inspection scheduling. Our clients don’t deal with the county at all.

WHICH LICENSE CLASS A BATHROOM REMODEL REQUIRES

Most bathroom remodels don’t require a Class A contractor, and license classes are commonly misrepresented on this point. Under Virginia law, Class A applies to single projects of $150,000 or more, Class B covers $30,000 to just under $150,000, and Class C covers work from just over $1,000 up to $30,000, so a typical bathroom sits in Class B territory on project value alone. Those thresholds were raised effective July 1, 2025, so older figures still circulating online are wrong. Boss Design Center holds a Virginia Class A license, the top tier. Read it as a signal of the scale of work a firm is set up to handle rather than as a legal requirement at bathroom price points.

HOW TO READ A BATHROOM REMODEL ESTIMATE

If you’re holding two or three quotes right now, the most useful thing you can do is stop comparing the bottom-line numbers and start comparing how the numbers were built.

Look for allowances. An allowance is a placeholder amount for something you haven’t chosen yet. A quote with a “$6,000 tile allowance” hasn’t priced your tile. It has reserved a space for a price you’ll find out later, after you’re committed. We cover how fixed-rate and cost-plus contracts differ on this point in more depth.

Check whether the wet area is itemized. Waterproofing, pan construction, drain and membrane should appear as specified work. If the shower is one line that says “shower,” the assembly underneath it hasn’t been priced.

Ask what happens if the layout moves. If the fixture locations in the drawing aren’t final, ask in writing what a change costs. That answer is much easier to get before you sign.

Ask who pulls the permits, and whose schedule the inspections sit on.

Ask what triggers a change order. There are legitimate answers here. Structural damage found after demolition has to be addressed, and scope you add yourself has to be priced. Anything beyond those two is worth questioning.

The estimate that ends up costing you the most is usually the one with the fewest decisions made in it, whatever its bottom line says on the day you receive it. If you want the wider version of this, we wrote a full guide on avoiding cost overruns on a remodeling project.

GET A REAL NUMBER BEFORE DEMOLITION STARTS

Every one of these costs can be settled in advance. The drain route, the waterproofing assembly, the tile pattern and its labor, the vanity, the fixtures and the permits can all be specified and priced before anyone picks up a hammer. It just takes doing that work during design instead of during construction.

That’s how we run every bathroom remodel. You select every material at our McLean showroom at 1389 Chain Bridge Road before we start, from the tile and grout color down to the hardware, and we produce photorealistic 3D renderings so you see the finished room before you commit to it. Then we write a fixed-rate contract with no allowances. If your project starts at a number, it ends at that number, with change orders reserved for structural conditions found after demolition and for scope you ask us to add. The finished work carries a five-year warranty on structural elements and one year on everything else.

If you’re planning a bathroom in Fairfax, Arlington, Loudoun or anywhere else in Northern Virginia, get in touch and we’ll walk your space, talk through what your layout actually requires, and turn a rough budget into a real number.

KITCHEN REMODEL PHASES AND WHAT TO EXPECT AT EACH STAGE
KITCHEN REMODEL PHASES AND WHAT TO EXPECT AT EACH STAGE
by Talha Gursoy Kitchen July 18, 2026

A full kitchen remodel moves through three phases: design, pre-construction, and construction. From your first consultation to a finished kitchen, the whole process usually takes about 6 to 8 months. Most of that time goes into planning and deciding, not living through demolition. The disruptive part, when your kitchen is actually torn out and rebuilt, is a much shorter window inside the construction phase.

That distinction matters, because most advice about kitchen remodels tells you to brace for chaos: budget a large contingency for surprises, expect change orders, prepare for decisions to keep coming at you mid-build. At Boss Design Center, a design-build firm working across the D.C. metro area since 2014, our process is built to remove that version of the experience. We settle every design and material decision before demolition begins, which is what lets us hold a fixed price and run construction on a schedule instead of a series of interruptions. This guide walks through each phase as it actually unfolds, what decisions happen when, and where the real surprises can and cannot show up.

THE THREE PHASES OF A KITCHEN REMODEL AT A GLANCE

Here is the full sequence and roughly how long each phase takes. The numbers below reflect a significant kitchen remodeling project, the kind that involves new cabinetry, new countertops, and updated plumbing and electrical.

Kitchen Remodeling Timeline: From First Consultation to Finished Kitchen
Typical phase-by-phase timeline for a full kitchen remodel
PHASE	TYPICAL TIMELINE	WHAT HAPPENS
Design	1 to 2 months	Consultation, measurements, complete material selection, 3D renderings, revisions
Pre-construction	4 to 6 weeks	Permits, material ordering, final scheduling, meeting your project team
Construction	3 to 4 months	Demolition, rough-in and inspections, installation, finishing, walkthrough
Total	About 6 to 8 months	First consultation to a finished kitchen

Timelines vary with the scope of the work. Structural changes, such as removing a load-bearing wall or reworking the footprint, push every number up. For a closer look at where the time goes, we cover it in our guide to how long a remodel takes.

One thing worth knowing before you start: national survey data shows that kitchens carry the longest planning timeline of any room in a home. The 2024 U.S. Houzz and Home Study found that homeowners spent far more time planning their kitchen renovations than building them. The longest stretch of a kitchen project is the planning, which is the part you have the most control over.

PHASE 1: DESIGN (1 TO 2 MONTHS)

The design phase is where you make every decision. This is deliberate. The more that gets settled now, the more predictable everything after it becomes.

THE INITIAL CONSULTATION

The process starts with an in-home consultation. Someone comes to see your actual space, takes in how you use it, and talks through what is and isn’t working: the lighting, the traffic flow, the storage, the layout problems you live with every day. This is also a budget conversation. Being upfront about what you want to spend prevents the far more painful experience of falling in love with a design you can’t afford to build.

At our showrooms, that first consultation is free, and we treat it partly as a fit check for both sides. You’re about to invest heavily and spend the better part of a year working with this team, so it should feel right.

ESTABLISHING THE DESIGN

Good kitchen design starts with the feeling you want, not the finishes. Many of the homeowners we work with bring inspiration images, and the useful question isn’t “what do you like about this photo” but “what does this photo make you feel.” Someone who says “I like the countertop color” is telling you one thing. Someone who says “I like how calm that kitchen feels” is telling you something much more useful about the whole space.

From there, a design philosophy takes shape: modern, traditional, transitional, or something specific to your home and your story. Once that direction is set, every later choice can be measured against it.

SELECTING EVERY MATERIAL

This is the step that separates a smooth remodel from a stressful one. During design, you select everything. Not just cabinets and countertops, but the backsplash tile, the grout color, the flooring, the fixtures, the appliances, the paint, the cabinet hardware, down to the outlet covers. Every finish gets chosen before anyone swings a hammer.

Choosing materials in a showroom, where you can see and touch the actual products under real light, beats approving them from small samples or a screen. It’s also why we can source 99 percent of the materials for a project ourselves, which keeps quality, timing, and warranty coverage under one roof.

PHOTOREALISTIC 3D RENDERINGS

Once the design and materials are locked, you get photorealistic 3D renderings of the finished kitchen. Not rough sketches or basic models, but accurate visualizations showing your exact cabinet configuration and color, your countertop’s real pattern, how light moves through the room, and how the whole space will feel.

This answers the question that weighs on people most during design: will it actually look like I pictured. You get to walk through your finished kitchen before a single thing is demolished, and you can request revisions until it’s right. The goal is that nothing about the finished result is a surprise, because you already saw it.

PHASE 2: PRE-CONSTRUCTION (4 TO 6 WEEKS)

With the design finalized, the project moves into pre-construction. Nothing gets torn out yet. This phase is about permits, ordering, and scheduling, the invisible work that makes construction run cleanly.

PERMITS

Kitchen remodels that touch plumbing, electrical, or mechanical systems require building and trade permits, and no legitimate work should happen without them. Across the D.C. metro, this is handled at the county level. Fairfax County, for example, requires permits and inspections during construction for renovations that alter these systems. Montgomery County has similar requirements through its residential alterations process.

We pull and manage all of these permits, including building, electrical, and plumbing, so you’re not navigating county portals or scheduling inspections yourself.

MATERIAL ORDERING AND CABINET LEAD TIMES

This is where the material choices you made during design pay off, because now we can order everything. Cabinetry is almost always the piece the whole schedule waits on, and custom cabinetry in particular takes real time to build. Across the industry, lead times generally fall in these ranges:

Cabinet Lead Times by Type
General ranges from order to delivery; your exact lead time is confirmed during material selection
CABINET TYPE	TYPICAL LEAD TIME
Stock	1 to 3 weeks
Semi-custom	4 to 8 weeks
Custom	8 to 14 weeks

These are general ranges, and they shift with season and supply. Spring and summer demand tends to lengthen the queue, which is exactly why we place your cabinet order now rather than mid-build. If you’re considering European cabinetry, the same logic applies. Our German kitchens carry their own manufacturing timelines that have to be planned for early.

Cabinetry is also usually the single largest line in a kitchen budget. The National Kitchen and Bath Association’s long-standing budgeting guideline puts cabinetry and hardware at roughly 29 percent of the total, and neutral sources like This Old House put cabinets at close to 30 percent. Because cabinets drive both the schedule and the budget, locking that decision early is the most important move in the whole process. We break down where the money goes in our guide to the most expensive part of a kitchen remodel.

MEETING YOUR PROJECT TEAM AND FINAL SCHEDULING

Before construction starts, you meet the project manager and coordinator who will run your build. In a design-build model, the designer who’s been with you since the first consultation stays involved through completion, so you’re not handed off to a separate crew that has to relearn your vision.

This is also where the fixed-rate contract earns its keep. Because every material is already selected and every cost already calculated, the quoted price holds. If a project is quoted at $200,000, it costs $200,000 at the end. Not $200,000 plus allowances, plus the “we’ll pick that out later” items that quietly inflate a bill. Front-loading the decisions is what makes that possible, and it’s the most reliable way to avoid cost overruns on a remodel.

PHASE 3: CONSTRUCTION (3 TO 4 MONTHS)

Construction is what most people picture when they think about a remodel, and it runs in a strict order dictated by physics and by code. You can’t template a countertop before the cabinets are installed, and you can’t close up a wall before it passes inspection. Understanding that sequence explains most of the “why does this take so long” questions.

DEMOLITION AND PREPARATION

Demolition is loud, dusty, and fast, often the quickest stage of the whole project. Before it starts, we protect the areas of your home that aren’t being touched with barriers and dust containment, and we clean up the site daily. This is the stage where living through the remodel feels most real, and we’ll come back to how to handle that below.

Demolition is also the one point where real surprises can appear. A decisions-first process removes the surprises that come from unmade decisions, but it can’t see through walls. In older homes, which are common across Northern Virginia, D.C., and Maryland, opening up a kitchen can reveal outdated or unsafe wiring, corroded old pipes, missing venting for the range hood, water damage, or past unpermitted work. Modern code also calls for updated electrical safety protections on kitchen circuits that older kitchens rarely have.

This is the honest exception to a no-surprises remodel. If something concealed turns up that has to be corrected for safety or code, that’s one of only two situations where a change order is warranted. The other is a change you request yourself. Everything else has already been priced.

ROUGH-IN AND INSPECTION

With demolition done, the rough-in work goes in: plumbing, electrical, and HVAC, plus any structural modifications like new beams or supports. This is the skeleton of your new kitchen, all the systems that will live behind the finished walls.

Before any of it gets covered up, it has to pass a rough-in inspection. This is a mandatory code step, not a firm-specific preference or an optional delay. A county inspector confirms the plumbing, mechanical, and electrical work meets code before insulation and drywall go in. Think of the inspection as protection rather than a holdup. It’s your assurance that the work hidden inside your walls was done right.

INSTALLATION, IN THE RIGHT ORDER

Installation follows a fixed sequence, and the order isn’t arbitrary:

Cabinets go in first, leveled and secured.

Countertops are templated only after the cabinets are set. Fabricators measure against the installed cabinets, not the plans, because templating from drawings produces fit problems. Stone fabrication then typically runs about 1 to 2 weeks.

Counters are installed, followed by the sink and faucet.

Backsplash, flooring, fixtures, lighting, and appliances complete the room.

That cabinet-then-countertop order is the clearest illustration of why the schedule can’t be rushed, and why the cabinet order placed back in pre-construction sets the pace for everything after it. Your cabinet style is chosen well before this stage. Whether you’re drawn to sleek flat-panel doors or classic shaker cabinets, that decision was locked during design so installation can move without pauses.

FINISHING AND THE FINAL WALKTHROUGH

The last stage is finishing: paint touch-ups, hardware, final details, and a thorough cleanup. Then comes the walkthrough. You and your project team go through the finished kitchen together and create a punch list of anything that needs correcting, however small. The project isn’t considered done until every punch list item is completed. This is the moment the renderings you approved months earlier become the room you’re standing in.

HOW YOU’LL KNOW WHAT’S HAPPENING DURING CONSTRUCTION

The most common worry during a build is losing visibility: not knowing what’s happening, when, or whether things are on track. A well-run process keeps you informed without you having to chase anyone.

During construction, you meet weekly with your project manager and coordinator, and you have real-time access to your project’s schedule, progress, and communication through an online system called BuilderTrend. You can check where things stand any time, rather than waiting for a phone call. Proactive updates are the standard, so questions get answered before you have to ask them.

LIVING IN YOUR HOME DURING A KITCHEN REMODEL

For a single-room kitchen remodel, most homeowners stay in their homes throughout. You lose your kitchen for a stretch, but not your house. The keys to making that livable:

Set up a temporary kitchen in a spot away from the construction dust, near an outlet and a water source. A dining room, basement, or laundry area works well.

Stock it with the basics: a microwave, a toaster oven or air fryer, an electric kettle, a portable induction burner, a coffee maker, and your relocated refrigerator.

Use a bathroom, laundry, or utility sink for washing up during the short window when the kitchen sink is out.

Keep an essentials box unpacked: a few knives, a cutting board, and your everyday spices.

Budget for extra takeout, and freeze a few meals in advance for the busiest stretches.

Protecting the rest of your home and cleaning up daily keeps the disruption contained to the room being renovated. Construction should stay a project happening in one part of your house, not something that takes over your whole life.

WHAT TO EXPECT, PHASE BY PHASE, IN SHORT

Design (1 to 2 months): You make every decision, from layout to outlet covers, and see it all in photorealistic renderings before anything is built.

Pre-construction (4 to 6 weeks): Permits are pulled, materials are ordered around cabinet lead times, and your price is locked.

Construction (3 to 4 months): Demolition, rough-in and inspection, then installation in the right order, ending in a walkthrough and punch list.

Total: about 6 to 8 months, most of it planning rather than demolition.

The later phases stay predictable because of the work done in the earlier ones. When every material is chosen, every cost is calculated, and every detail is visualized before demolition, construction becomes execution instead of a running series of decisions.

PLANNING A KITCHEN REMODEL IN THE D.C. METRO AREA?

If you’re considering a kitchen remodel in Northern Virginia, Maryland, or D.C., the best first step is a conversation about your space, your goals, and your budget. We offer a free in-home consultation, and you’re welcome to visit our McLean or Bethesda showroom to see materials in person and get a feel for how we work. Reach out to Boss Design Center to start your design.

FIXED-RATE VS. COST-PLUS CONTRACTS FOR REMODELING (2026)
FIXED-RATE VS. COST-PLUS CONTRACTS FOR REMODELING (2026)
by Talha Gursoy Boss Design Update July 13, 2026

When you gather bids for a kitchen or whole house remodel, you’ll run into two very different ways contractors price the work. A fixed-rate contract (also called fixed-price or lump-sum) gives you one total price for the whole project, agreed before construction starts. A cost-plus contract bills you for the actual cost of labor and materials as the job proceeds, plus the contractor’s fee, so the final number stays open until the work is done. The real difference between them comes down to one question: who carries the risk if the project costs more than expected?

That question has an honest answer, and it depends on your project. At Boss Design Center, we’ve been running design-build remodels across the D.C. metro area since 2014, mostly kitchens in the $80,000 to $250,000 range, and we price every job as a fixed rate with no allowances. So we have a clear point of view. But cost-plus is the right structure for some projects, and this guide weighs both fairly: how each one works, where your money is exposed, and the conditions where each one actually fits. Keep one thing in mind as you read. A fixed price only protects you if it’s built on a complete design. Without that, a “fixed” price is an estimate waiting to move.

WHAT IS A FIXED-RATE REMODELING CONTRACT?

A fixed-rate contract sets one total price for a defined scope of work, agreed before construction begins. The contractor is paid that amount regardless of what the work actually costs to complete, which means the contractor absorbs the risk if materials or labor come in higher than planned.

A fixed price is only as reliable as the design behind it. When every selection is made and priced before you sign, the number is real. When the contract is full of placeholder figures for decisions you haven’t made yet, the “fixed” price will move once those decisions get made.

HOW ALLOWANCES TURN A FIXED PRICE INTO A MOVING ONE

This is where a lot of “fixed” quotes quietly come apart. Many contractors write allowances into the contract: placeholder amounts for items you’ll choose later. A contract might list a $10,000 allowance for countertops with the plan to pick them during construction. Then you’re midway through the project, committed to the contractor, and the counters you actually want cost $15,000. Now you’re facing a $5,000 increase you never budgeted for.

We reject that approach. On our projects, every detail is selected and priced during the design phase before construction starts: cabinets, countertop material and edge, backsplash tile and grout, flooring, fixtures, hardware, paint, down to the outlet covers. If we quote your kitchen at $200,000, it ends at $200,000. No allowances, no mid-project true-ups.

WHAT IS A COST-PLUS REMODELING CONTRACT?

A cost-plus contract works the opposite way. You reimburse the contractor for the actual cost of labor and materials as they’re incurred, then pay an added fee on top for overhead and profit. The final total isn’t set at signing. It’s tallied from real invoices as the work gets done, which means the budget stays open until completion. According to Investopedia, that structure shifts most of the financial risk of overruns onto the owner, since actual costs are reimbursed whatever they turn out to be.

The fee (the “plus”) is usually structured one of two ways: a flat fixed fee agreed up front, or a percentage of the total project cost. Some cost-plus contracts add a guaranteed maximum price, or GMP, which caps what you’ll pay and hands any overage above the cap back to the contractor. Cost-plus is sometimes confused with time-and-materials billing. The difference is that time-and-materials charges pre-set hourly rates, while cost-plus reimburses documented actual costs plus the defined fee.

Done well, cost-plus is transparent. You see the real invoices, and an open-book contractor gives you line-item visibility into where your money goes. It also flexes easily when the scope changes, because a change simply adds to the reimbursable total instead of triggering a formal renegotiation.

WHO CARRIES THE RISK OF GOING OVER BUDGET?

This is the heart of the comparison. Under a fixed-rate contract, the contractor carries the risk of an overrun. Under a cost-plus contract, most of that risk sits with you, because you’re paying actual costs no matter where they land.

Overruns are common enough that this matters. In the 2026 U.S. Houzz & Home Study, the largest published survey of residential remodeling activity, 37% of homeowners exceeded their planned spend in 2025, while only 35% came in on budget. The most common reasons were higher-than-expected product and service costs, pricier materials than planned, and expanding scope mid-renovation.

Look closely at that list. Most of it is decisions and selections. Under a genuine fixed price, those choices are already made and locked before the contract is signed, so they can’t move the number. Under cost-plus, every one of them lands on your invoice.

THE INCENTIVE PROBLEM WITH PERCENTAGE-BASED COST-PLUS

Percentage-based cost-plus has a structural quirk worth understanding. When the fee is a percentage of cost, the contractor earns more in absolute dollars every time the project gets more expensive. Spending more raises their fee, so the pricing model gives them no built-in reason to hold costs down.

The federal government takes this seriously enough to ban the structure in its own contracting. Cost-plus-a-percentage-of-cost contracts are prohibited by federal law precisely because a fee that rises with spending removes the incentive to control costs.

To be fair, that criticism applies only to the percentage version. A cost-plus contract with a flat fixed fee removes the problem, because the fee doesn’t rise with costs. A guaranteed maximum price caps your exposure. Plenty of reputable contractors use cost-plus with a fixed fee or a GMP precisely to keep their incentives aligned with yours. If you’re weighing a cost-plus bid, the fee structure is the first thing to check.

FIXED-RATE VS. COST-PLUS CONTRACTS AT A GLANCE
Fixed-rate vs. cost-plus remodeling contracts at a glance
How the two pricing structures compare on risk, transparency, and fit
FACTOR	FIXED-RATE (FIXED-PRICE)	COST-PLUS
How the price is set	One total price for a defined scope, agreed before construction	Actual costs billed as work happens, plus a fee
Final cost known before you sign	Yes, when the design is complete	No, the total stays open until completion
Who carries overrun risk	The contractor	Mostly the homeowner
Contractor’s cost incentive	Strong reason to control costs	Weak under a percentage fee, better with a fixed fee or GMP
Cost transparency	Priced against selected materials up front	Open-book, actual invoices as you go
Handles evolving scope	Works best when scope is fully defined	Flexes easily as scope changes
Best fit	A designable project where you want cost certainty	Undefined scope, major unknowns, or an owner managing the job
WHEN COST-PLUS IS THE RIGHT CHOICE

Cost-plus earns its place when the scope genuinely can’t be pinned down before work starts. A few situations where it fits:

Undefined or evolving scope, where the design is still taking shape as the project moves.
Major structural unknowns, like a gut renovation of an older home where nobody knows what’s behind the walls until demolition.
Volatile input prices, where locking a fixed number means paying for the contractor’s risk buffer whether or not it’s needed.
Experienced owner-managers and investors who run their own design and sourcing and would rather pay actual cost than a built-in premium.

In those cases, the flexibility and open-book pricing of cost-plus are real advantages, and a fixed price would either be impossible to set honestly or would cost you a premium you don’t need to pay.

WHY 2026 MATERIAL AND LABOR COSTS ARE PART OF THIS DECISION

There’s a legitimate argument for cost-plus grounded in current data. When input prices are moving, a fixed-price contractor has to build a contingency into the number to protect against increases. You pay for that buffer whether or not costs actually rise.

And prices are moving. Building material prices rose 3.5% year over year heading into 2026, the largest annual increase since early 2023, according to the National Association of Home Builders. The Associated General Contractors reports that the price index for nonresidential construction inputs climbed 3.6% over twelve months, with a majority of contractors naming materials costs as a top concern for the year, alongside worries about labor availability. In that environment, cost-plus lets an owner skip the risk premium and pay actual cost.

The trade-off is certainty. On a project you can fully design in advance, most homeowners we work with would rather know the exact number and let us carry the price risk. That’s a real decision with a cost on both sides, and it’s yours to make.

WHEN A FIXED-RATE CONTRACT MAKES SENSE

A fixed-rate contract is the stronger fit when two things are true: your project can be fully designed before construction, and you want to know the total before you commit. That covers most kitchen remodeling projects and whole house remodeling with a clear scope, and most homeowners who aren’t planning to manage the job themselves.

The condition that makes a fixed price real is complete upfront design. Every material and detail gets selected and priced during the design phase, and you see photorealistic 3D renderings of the finished space before anyone starts building. The price is set against the actual materials you chose, not placeholders. The design-build model matters here too. When the same team designs and builds, the designers understand construction costs and can price the job accurately from the start. That’s what makes a genuine fixed number possible.

An honest fixed rate isn’t a rigid one. On our projects, change orders happen in only two situations: structural damage we discover after demolition that has to be addressed for safety or code, and a change you request beyond the original agreed design. That’s what separates a real fixed price from a contract that pretends nothing will ever change, and it’s what makes the fixed number believable in the first place.

HOW TO TELL A REAL FIXED PRICE FROM A LOOSE ESTIMATE

Whichever direction you lean, the questions you ask while comparing bids matter more than the label on the contract. Before you sign anything, ask:

Are all materials and finishes selected and priced now, or are there allowances for decisions we’ll make later?
What specifically triggers a change order, and how are change orders priced?
Can I see the renderings, specs, or selections the price is built on?
If it’s cost-plus, is the fee a flat amount or a percentage of cost, and is there a guaranteed maximum price?
What does the payment schedule look like?

A contractor who can answer these clearly, and show you the selections behind the number, is giving you a price you can trust. A vague answer is a sign the number is likely to move.

FREQUENTLY ASKED QUESTIONS
IS A FIXED-PRICE CONTRACT ALWAYS CHEAPER THAN COST-PLUS?

Not necessarily. A fixed price may include a contingency to protect the contractor against rising costs, so on a smooth project cost-plus can come in lower. What a fixed price buys you is certainty: you know the number before you commit, and the contractor carries the risk if costs climb.

WHAT ARE ALLOWANCES, AND WHY DO THEY CAUSE OVERRUNS?

Allowances are placeholder dollar amounts a contractor writes into a contract for items you haven’t selected yet, like a set figure for countertops or tile. When your actual selection costs more than the allowance, the price is adjusted upward mid-project. That’s a frequent source of surprise increases, and it’s why we price every selection before construction instead of leaving it for later.

CAN A COST-PLUS CONTRACT HAVE A MAXIMUM PRICE?

Yes. A cost-plus contract with a guaranteed maximum price (GMP) caps the total you’ll pay. Costs above the cap become the contractor’s responsibility, which gives you some of the flexibility of cost-plus with a ceiling on your exposure.

WHAT’S THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN COST-PLUS AND TIME-AND-MATERIALS?

Both leave the final total open, but they bill differently. Time-and-materials charges pre-set hourly labor rates plus materials. Cost-plus reimburses the contractor’s documented actual costs and adds a defined fee for overhead and profit.

GET A FIXED PRICE YOU CAN PLAN AROUND
